evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(sale, 3), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

evaluated.reasoning: This targets the specific known weakness of Graham-style normalization — backward-looking averages flatter shrinking firms — with a conditioner that is not a profitability level, trend, volatility or durability measure but the trajectory of the business base itself, so it is a new moderator dimension for this archive. If it lifts alpha above the champion, the residual risk in normalized value is decline rather than distress, which would redirect the remaining generations toward growth-guarded normalization rather than further quality gates.

evaluated.name: AssetLightness_x_DemonstratedEarningPowerYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MAX(oiadp, MA(oiadp, 5)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The right anchor for value is a firm's demonstrated earning capacity, defined as the greater of what it earns today and its own mid-cycle norm: the norm rescues firms in a temporary trough, while current profit rescues firms whose five-year average is stale because the business has genuinely improved, and cheapness against that anchor is the mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not the negation of the archived shortfall signal, whose result is mechanically known — the MAX anchor is a non-linear envelope of the two proven components rather than their difference or their sum, so it is not recoverable from any previously evaluated expression. It also encodes a specific economic asymmetry the archive has not tested: the averaged anchor and the spot anchor each fail for an identifiable group of firms, and the envelope fails for neither, which should raise the slope without the coverage cost of extra conditioning.

evaluated.name: PerShareEarningPowerGrowth_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 3), csho), 3), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Only earning power per share accrues to existing owners, so cheapness against mid-cycle profit is real value when smoothed operating profit per share has been rising, and largely illusory when aggregate profit grew only because the share base was expanded to fund it.
evaluated.reasoning: The mechanism is now stated in the direction the arithmetic actually runs: dividing smoothed profit by the *current* share count each year and taking its three-year growth mechanically penalizes firms that issued equity and rewards those that retired stock, which is the opposite of averaging stale per-share history. The moderator is a profitability trajectory measured at the owner level rather than per asset — a conditioner dimension not yet tested — and it is paired with the archive's best valuation leg so the comparison against the champion isolates the dilution-adjusted growth channel.

evaluated.name: RevenueScaledCapitalIntensity_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, sale))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically relevant burden is capital consumption per dollar of revenue produced, not per dollar of book assets, because revenue measures the output the capital base actually generates and is immune to the write-downs and stale historical cost that distort the asset denominator.
evaluated.reasoning: The champion's weight is the one component never varied, and the critic's standing objection is that dp/at is a noisy proxy contaminated by asset-base accounting; scaling the same capital-consumption charge by revenue tests whether the effect is about the business model's reinvestment need or about the asset denominator. Coverage is unaffected because both inputs are already required by the champion.

evaluated.name: CapitalProductivity_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness against mid-cycle earning power pays most for firms that turn their capital over quickly, because high asset turnover means the earning power is generated by an efficient operating base rather than by a heavy, slow-moving asset stock whose returns are hostage to utilization.
evaluated.reasoning: Turnover and depreciation intensity are economically distinct readings of "capital-light" — one is productivity of the asset base, the other its consumption rate — and separating them tells us which mechanism drives the archive's best result. This is the sharper of the two interpretations to test because turnover is a first-order operating characteristic rather than an accounting charge, and it is measurable for every firm without additional lags.

evaluated.name: AssetLightness_x_ConservativeEarningPowerYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MIN(oiadp, MA(oiadp, 5)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A prudent valuation anchor is the lower of current and mid-cycle profit: a firm that still looks cheap on the pessimistic estimate of its earning power is cheap for real, whereas a firm that looks cheap only because a stale five-year average flatters a deteriorating business, or only because of one exceptional year, is not.
evaluated.reasoning: The MAX envelope (demonstrated capability) delivered 3.0% alpha and the plain average 3.4%, so the untested lower envelope directly answers whether the champion's edge comes from optimistic capability or from conservatism, and it is not recoverable from either parent since MIN is a different non-linear function of the same two inputs. Economically it screens out the two failure modes of normalization — stale averages for decliners and windfall years — using no additional data.

evaluated.name: FiveYearCashValidation_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 5), at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Averaged accounting profit is only a credible measure of earning power if, over the very same five years, that profit converted into operating cash; firms that accumulated accruals over the window have a flattered average and their apparent normalized cheapness is an accounting artifact.

Cumulative accruals are also a stronger and more persistent predictor than one-year accruals, which is the reason to accept the coverage cost of a five-year cash-flow window.

evaluated.name: AssetLightness_x_TroughEarningPowerYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_MIN(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Value with a margin of safety means being cheap against the profit a firm earns in its worst year, not its average year; pricing the five-year trough of operating profit against market value ranks firms by stress-tested earning power and automatically pushes firms whose worst year was a loss to the expensive end where they belong.
evaluated.reasoning: This achieves the distress-screening intent of the flagged proposal inside the signed valuation leg rather than by silently deleting firms, so coverage matches the champion and no sample-selection shift confounds the comparison — firms with a negative trough receive strongly negative scores instead of vanishing. It is also a distinct anchor from both the mean and the current-versus-mean lower envelope, because the trough is a worst-case order statistic that reveals cyclical fragility the average conceals.

evaluated.name: AssetLightness_x_NormalizedResidualEarningPowerYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(SUB(oiadp, xint), 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity owns mid-cycle operating profit only after lenders are paid, so pricing normalized operating profit against market capitalization systematically overstates the cheapness of levered firms; netting the interest bill out of normal earning power measures the residual claim shareholders actually buy, and the correction is largest precisely for the levered value names that trap value investors.
evaluated.reasoning: No prior signal nets financing costs out of a normalized *equity* yield: the archive either priced operating profit against equity alone, which mismatches numerator and denominator claims, or against total capital, which prices the whole structure and so cannot identify equity-specific mispricing. Holding the capital-intensity weight fixed isolates this claim-matching correction, and it should raise both the slope and the alpha if the champion's long leg has been partly populated by levered firms whose apparent cheapness belongs to their creditors.

evaluated.name: LighteningCapitalBase_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3), 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose capital-consumption burden is falling are transitioning toward a lighter business model in which a growing share of mid-cycle profit becomes distributable; the market prices the historical capital intensity rather than its trajectory, so cheap firms in the middle of that transition are underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: The level of capital intensity is the archive's most productive conditioner, yet its direction of travel has never been examined, and the two are economically distinct: the level says what the business is, the change says what it is becoming. Smoothing over three years before differencing keeps the measure from reacting to a single year of depreciation-schedule noise, and coverage is essentially that of the champion.

evaluated.name: VariableCostFlexibility_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(cogs, ADD(cogs, xsga))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A low multiple on mid-cycle earning power is compensation for fundamental risk when the cost base is rigid, because a fixed overhead structure converts a demand shock into a loss, whereas a firm whose costs are predominantly variable can shrink with its revenue and preserve the earning power the multiple is discounting.
evaluated.reasoning: Cost-structure flexibility is an economically distinct conditioner from capital intensity — one concerns how much of the profit is reinvested in assets, the other how much of the cost base can be switched off — and it is the channel that best explains why cheap firms become traps in recessions. The construction repairs the earlier overhead attempt that was flagged as unstable: the share of variable costs in total costs has two strictly positive components, is bounded in the unit interval, and cannot flip sign for distressed firms with collapsed gross profit.

evaluated.reasoning: Every profitability conditioner tested so far — level, trend, acceleration, durability, volatility, accruals, capital intensity — is a property of the average or existing business, whereas the marginal return on new capital is a different economic quantity and the one that governs whether normalized earning power will persist or grow. The five-year differencing window matches the horizon of the valuation anchor, and both winsorization and industry ranking contain the cases where the incremental asset base is small.

evaluated.name: UnencumberedEarningPower_x_NormalizedEarningsYield

evaluated.hypothesis: Mid-cycle operating profit belongs to shareholders only to the extent that it is not pledged to lenders; a firm cheap on normal earning power with a lightly levered balance sheet offers that earning power unencumbered, whereas the same multiple on a heavily indebted firm prices a residual claim that a single bad year can extinguish.

It is also distinct from the interest-coverage conditioner tested earlier, which measures the current ability to service debt from flows rather than the size of the prior claim on the asset base, and it interacts specifically with an equity-priced yield whose numerator ignores that claim.

evaluated.hypothesis: The credibility of a five-year average as an estimate of earning power depends on how large that average is relative to its own year-to-year dispersion; firms with a high ratio of mean to standard deviation of return on capital have earning power that can actually be relied upon, so their low multiples are informative while noisy firms' averages are not.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not the volatility conditioner tested earlier — that one penalized dispersion irrespective of the level of profitability and produced only 0.9% alpha, whereas the mean-to-dispersion ratio is the estimator's own signal-to-noise and treats a stable 3% return very differently from a stable 20% return. It targets the specific statistical weakness of the whole normalized-yield family, namely that the anchor is an estimate whose reliability varies enormously across firms, and it uses a scale-free return-on-assets basis so it is not mechanically tied to the price-scaled valuation leg.

evaluated.hypothesis: For firms that build their competitive position through expensed selling, marketing and development spending, operating income understates earning power because it charges investment as cost; mid-cycle gross profit is the cleaner anchor, so cheapness measured against normalized gross profit identifies mispricing that an operating-income multiple misses.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a claim about which income line represents earning power in an economy where intangible investment runs through the expense base, not another rescaling of the same line: gross profit is pre-investment and pre-overhead-accounting-choice, and the difference between the two anchors is largest exactly for the intangible-intensive firms the market misvalues. Holding the capital-intensity weight fixed at the champion's makes the anchor change the only moving part, and coverage is unaffected since both revenue and cost of goods are as widely reported as operating income.

evaluated.hypothesis: Mid-cycle operating profit is produced by the operating business, not by the cash pile, so it should be priced against the market value of the operating business alone; cash-rich firms are systematically misclassified as expensive by an unadjusted market-cap denominator even though the price of their operations is far lower.

evaluated.hypothesis: Growth that is bought with price cuts is worthless, and margin gains achieved by shrinking the business are worse; a cheap firm is genuinely underpriced when it has expanded its revenue base *and* held or improved its operating margin at the same time, which is the observable signature of pricing power.

It attacks the documented weakness of backward-looking normalization (flattering decliners) without simply betting on growth, since the growth leg is neutralized whenever margins are deteriorating.

evaluated.reasoning: This introduces the distribution channel — a variable and an economic mechanism the archive has never used successfully — while avoiding the artifact that sank the earlier attempt: the conditioner is a graded consistency count rather than a dividend yield, so non-payers receive a neutral zero weight instead of being dumped into the short leg, and the spread is still cheap-versus-expensive rather than payers-versus-non-payers. It is also not mechanically linked to the price denominator, unlike any yield-based payout conditioner.

evaluated.name: InnovationPersistence_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_COUNT(xrd, 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that consistently spend on research have their earning power understated by accounting that expenses that spending as it occurs, so when such a firm already looks cheap on mid-cycle operating profit its true economic yield is higher still and the mispricing is larger than the multiple suggests.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the internally inconsistent double-depreciation construct with a coherent cross-theme conditioner built on the one profitability variable the archive has never used, and the reporting-persistence count is the construction the task guidance explicitly sanctions for R&D: it distinguishes firms with a sustained innovation programme from occasional reporters without discarding non-reporters, who receive a neutral zero weight so coverage is preserved. It is economically distinct from the accumulated-SG&A intangible proxy tested earlier, which mixes overhead with investment, because R&D is unambiguously investment.

evaluated.name: CapitalEfficientGrowth_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(sale, 5), GROWTH(at, 5)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Growth that outpaces the balance sheet is growth the existing asset base delivered; when a cheap firm has expanded revenue faster than assets over five years, its mid-cycle earning power is scaling without absorbing new capital, whereas a cheap firm whose assets grew faster than sales is buying revenue and will not deliver that earning power to owners.
evaluated.reasoning: The sign pathology is eliminated at the source: both legs of the difference are growth rates of strictly positive quantities, so no firm can be ranked as disciplined because its cumulative profit was negative. It is also not the asset-growth anomaly in disguise — a firm growing assets rapidly can rank highly provided revenue grew faster — which is precisely the difference between the investment factor and the capital-efficiency mechanism this tests.

evaluated.name: LiquidityBuffer_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness only pays if the firm survives long enough for mid-cycle earning power to reassert itself; a liquid balance sheet is the insurance that lets a cheap firm ride out the trough without a dilutive rescue, so the value premium should be concentrated among cheap firms holding a real cash buffer.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the collinear DuPont conjunction — which could not have discriminated between competing explanations of the champion — with a survivability channel that is orthogonal to profitability measures entirely, and it is structurally different from the failed net-cash-to-price signal: cash enters as a bounded balance-sheet conditioner rather than as the valuation numerator, so the signal cannot be hijacked by tiny cash-burning firms whose net cash dominates their market value. Together with the accepted operating-business-price proposal it separates two distinct roles for cash: correcting the price of operations versus insuring the operating business.

evaluated.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, at), NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness against mid-cycle earning power pays most where the asset base is liquid and lightly depreciating, because such a firm neither surrenders its profit to replacement capital nor depends on outside money to reach the recovery; cash holdings and low capital consumption are two independent readings of that same balance-sheet condition.
evaluated.reasoning: The two best signals in the archive use these two conditioners separately (3.6% and 3.4% alpha), and SUMRANK adds their ranks rather than multiplying them, which avoids the cross-sectional compression that cut alpha when two bounded weights were multiplied together in generation 5. Coverage is the archive's maximum because both inputs are universally reported alongside the five-year profit average.

evaluated.name: LiquidAndAssetLight_Conjunction_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The two balance-sheet conditions are jointly necessary rather than substitutable: a cash-rich firm whose operations still devour capital, and a capital-light firm with no liquidity to survive the trough, both fail to deliver mid-cycle earning power to owners, so the weaker of the two readings should govern.
evaluated.reasoning: Together with Signals 1 and 2 this completes a clean three-way test of how the two proven conditioners should be combined — additively, as one netted quantity, or conjunctively — and MIN is the only one of the three that cannot be reproduced by any linear function of the inputs. It is the appropriate structure if the mechanism is a survival-and-retention requirement rather than a graded characteristic.

evaluated.name: LiquidityBuffer_x_OperatingBusinessPriceYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MAX(SUB(MUL(prcc_f, csho), che), ceq)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: If the cash conditioner works because the market underprices balance-sheet cash, then removing cash from the price should absorb the effect; if it works because liquidity is insurance that lets a cheap firm survive to realize its earning power, then removing cash from the price should sharpen it by measuring the operating business more accurately.

It matters for the final recommendation because a mispricing-of-cash interpretation and an insurance interpretation imply different exposures and different robustness out of sample.

evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What protects a cheap firm is not gross cash but its liquidity relative to the claims against it: the share of cash in cash-plus-debt measures whether the firm's financial position lets it wait out a downturn, and cheapness should pay in proportion to that slack.

evaluated.name: CapitalReplacementRunway_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, dp), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The balance-sheet condition that protects normalized cheapness is how many years of capital replacement a firm could fund from cash already in hand; a cheap firm with several years of runway will reach the recovery in its mid-cycle earning power without raising outside money, while one whose cash covers only months of capital consumption must dilute or borrow first.

Its portfolio will also be far less concentrated than the product's, so if it matches the product's alpha with a higher Sharpe the additive form is the better final recommendation, and if it falls materially short the interaction claim is confirmed.

considered.name: BookYield_Gated_By_Sustained_ROA
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), INDICATOR(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3), 0.05))
considered.hypothesis: Value premia are concentrated among firms with a multi-year record of adequate operating returns; cheap firms failing a persistent-profitability screen are value traps whose low price reflects genuine fundamental deterioration.
considered.reasoning: The three-year moving average of operating ROA measures sustained, not transitory, profitability, and the indicator switches the book-yield signal on only for firms clearing that hurdle. This is a conditional (state-dependent) use of valuation rather than a rescaled book-to-market, since all firms below the profitability threshold receive an identical neutral score.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DoubleScreen_ROE_CashFlowYield_Min
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, ceq)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: Only firms that clear both a profitability and a cheapness bar earn the joint premium; taking the weaker of the two within-industry ranks enforces conjunction so that extreme scores on one theme cannot compensate for weakness on the other.
considered.reasoning: An additive composite lets a hyper-profitable expensive stock or a distressed ultra-cheap stock enter the long leg, whereas the MIN operator admits only genuine profitable-value firms and places any single-theme failure in the short leg. Cash earnings (ib plus depreciation) in the yield leg keeps the valuation channel economically distinct from the accounting ROE leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValueTilt_Scaled_By_OperatingProfitability
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), xsga), at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The book-yield signal is informative in proportion to how profitable the firm is: among high operating-profitability firms a low price signals genuine mispricing (long) and a high price signals genuine over-pricing (short), whereas among unprofitable firms valuation carries little information and the position should be shrunk toward zero.
considered.reasoning: Replacing one z-score with a strictly non-negative industry rank in [0,1] removes the sign degeneracy the critic identified: the signed valuation leg alone determines the long/short side, and profitability only modulates its magnitude, so an unprofitable glamour firm now receives a score near zero rather than a large positive one. This is a slope-modulation (interaction) structure, not the additive quality-plus-value composite, because the value spread is mechanically compressed to zero at the bottom of the profitability distribution.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OwnHistoryDeRating_x_GrossProfitability
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5))
considered.hypothesis: A firm trading at the cheap end of its own five-year valuation range while still earning high production profits has been de-rated without fundamental justification, and this within-firm multiple contraction reverts; cross-sectionally cheap-but-unprofitable firms show no such reversion.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the published single-ratio construction and instead interacts a firm-relative (time-series) cheapness state with a cross-sectional profitability state, so neither leg can proxy for the other and neither reproduces a standard value or profitability sort. Both legs are bounded non-negative ranks, so the score is monotone increasing in each theme with no sign degeneracy, and the conjunctive curvature means high profitability only pays when the firm is also cheap versus its own history.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashFlowYield_Weighted_By_MarginImprovement
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness on operating cash flow pays only when the profitability path is improving; investors extrapolate the past decline that produced the low multiple, so the value premium is concentrated in firms whose five-year operating-return trend has already turned up, and is neutral where fundamentals are still deteriorating.
considered.reasoning: The valuation leg now uses operating cash flow instead of net income, which stays economically meaningful for loss-making firms and avoids the ill-behaved earnings-yield denominator problem. The profitability-trend leg enters as a non-negative rank weight, so improving-but-expensive firms are shorted and deteriorating firms are pulled toward zero rather than being pushed into the long leg, eliminating the sign degeneracy of the original z-score product.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SalesYield_x_ProfitYearCount
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ib, at), 0), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Sales-to-price is the most contrarian and least profitability-aware valuation measure, so it rewards investors only when the firm has demonstrated that revenue converts into earnings; the count of profitable years over five years grades that conversion reliability and amplifies the sales-yield spread.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the arithmetically additive rank difference with a graded multiplicative weight (0 to 5 profitable years) applied to a signed valuation z-score, so the two themes cannot be collapsed into an equal-weighted composite and firms with erratic profitability are neutralized rather than ranked. The mechanism is specifically about revenue-based cheapness being a trap absent persistent bottom-line profitability, which is distinct from any book-yield or earnings-yield screen.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SolvencyAdjustedProfit_x_EVYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oibdp, xint), at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(oiadp, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Enterprise-value cheapness is a mispricing only when operating profits comfortably exceed the interest burden; levered cheap firms are priced low because debtholders, not shareholders, own the profit stream.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are debt-aware in a way HML is not — the valuation leg prices operating income against equity plus net debt, and the profitability leg nets interest expense out of operating cash profit — so the signal should carry less mechanical HML/RMW loading and leave more residual FF5 alpha. The interaction is essential: neither an EV yield nor an interest-adjusted margin alone separates cheap-and-solvent from cheap-and-distressed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashBackedEarnings_x_CashEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A high earnings yield is trustworthy only if the reported earnings are backed by operating cash; cheap firms whose profits are accrual-inflated are pricing in a future writedown, while cheap firms with cash-backed profits are genuinely mispriced.
considered.reasoning: This introduces earnings quality as the profitability channel, which is a different economic content from the level-of-profitability channel that RMW spans, so it is the proposal most likely to produce FF5 alpha rather than factor loadings. The accrual leg enters as a bounded non-negative rank weight, so accrual-heavy firms are neutralized rather than flipped into the long leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProfitStability_x_CashEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The value premium is concentrated in firms with predictable operating returns; when profitability is volatile, a low price is compensation for fundamental risk rather than evidence of mispricing, so cheapness should be discounted in proportion to profit instability.
considered.reasoning: This uses the second moment of profitability rather than its level, a dimension RMW does not capture, so the resulting spread should be less spanned by FF5 and can separate genuine mispricing from risk-based cheapness. It directly tests the value-trap explanation for the weak long-short alphas in generation 0: if the cheap leg was contaminated by high-variance firms, stability weighting should raise both ls_alpha and ls_talpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GlamourMultiple_x_ProfitFade
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The profitability-value interaction is strongest on the expensive side: firms carrying rich price-to-book multiples whose smoothed operating returns have started to fall are priced for a growth path the fundamentals have already abandoned, and they underperform as expectations are marked down.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the archived "rank-weighted signed yield" template entirely — it is a product of two non-negative ranks with a negative expected sign, deliberately concentrating identification in the glamour-and-fading corner rather than the crowded cheap-and-profitable corner. Because FF5 gives no explicit factor for deteriorating profitability at high multiples, the short leg is the place where residual alpha is most likely to survive HML and RMW loadings, and the smoothed three-year base makes the deterioration term a genuine state change rather than one-year noise.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OverheadBurden_Gated_GrossProfitYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(xsga, SUB(revt, cogs)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Gross profit only reaches shareholders after overhead; a cheap stock with high production profit but a rigid selling and administrative cost base converts little of that profit into distributable earnings, so cheapness pays in proportion to how light the overhead burden is.
considered.reasoning: Unlike the flagged version, this cannot be multiplied out into a published multiple — the weight is a cost-structure ratio (overhead per dollar of gross profit) that is not a scaled profitability level, so the product is not EBIT/EV or any of its relatives. The economic channel is cost rigidity and operating leverage, which is distinct from both the interest-burden channel in the accepted EV proposal and the level-of-profitability content of RMW.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NetCashDiscount_x_OperatingProfitability
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The market discounts balance-sheet cash because it fears it will be consumed; when a firm holds large net cash relative to its market value and simultaneously earns strong operating returns, the cash is genuine unencumbered value rather than a burn buffer, and the discount reverses.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the dividend channel — which mechanically sorted payers against non-payers — with net-cash-to-price, a valuation measure that is defined and continuously distributed for every firm, including levered ones whose values are negative. The interaction is essential and not a standard screen: net cash alone is dominated by cash-burning biotech-style firms, and profitability alone says nothing about the balance sheet, so only the joint condition identifies a mispriced cash discount.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AssetLightness_x_EbitdaCapitalYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A low EBITDA multiple is an illusion for capital-hungry firms whose depreciation charge proxies the reinvestment needed just to stand still; the same multiple on an asset-light firm represents genuine distributable profit, so cheapness pays in inverse proportion to capital intensity.
considered.reasoning: Capital intensity is an economically distinct moderator from the level, trend, volatility, solvency and accrual channels already tested — it explains *why* a pre-depreciation multiple misprices, rather than measuring how good or reliable profits are. The valuation leg keeps the strictly positive total-capital denominator so the test is clean, and the interaction is essential because depreciation intensity alone is a sector proxy with no directional return content.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: StackedQualityGate_x_CashEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oibdp, xint), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The two conditions that separate genuine value from value traps are independent — a cheap firm must both service its debt from operating profit and report earnings that are backed by cash — so requiring the weaker of the two to be high should sharpen the spread beyond either moderator alone.
considered.reasoning: Solvency and accrual quality delivered the archive's two highest t-alphas (1.67 and 1.70) through economically different mechanisms, so this asks whether their information is complementary or redundant, a question no single-moderator variant can answer. The MIN operator enforces conjunction so that an excellent interest cover cannot excuse accrual-inflated earnings, and the weight remains bounded and non-negative so the signed yield leg alone determines the long and short sides.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OwnHistoryYieldDeRating_x_SolvencyProfit
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oibdp, xint), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5))
considered.hypothesis: A firm trading at the highest cash-earnings yield of its own five-year history while still covering its interest burden from operating profit has been de-rated without a solvency justification, and that firm-specific de-rating reverts.
considered.reasoning: Holding the moderator fixed at the best-performing solvency leg, this swaps the cross-sectional valuation state for a within-firm one, which is the single design change that produced positive alpha in generation 0 and which mechanically carries far less HML loading because it is neutral to a firm's permanent multiple level. The comparison against Signal 1 tells us whether the alpha in this family comes from cheapness in levels or from de-rating relative to a firm's own norm.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginExpansion_x_YieldReRating_Divergence
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: When a firm's cash-earnings yield rises (the market marks it down) at the same time as its gross margin expands, price and fundamentals have diverged, and the divergence closes in favour of the fundamentals.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are first differences rather than levels, which is a structurally new construction for this archive: it targets the *rate* at which expectations and profitability move apart instead of the static cheap-and-good corner, and is therefore close to orthogonal to HML and RMW by construction. The margin change is measured on gross margin so it reflects pricing power and cost pass-through rather than accounting overhead choices, and the interaction is essential because a rising yield alone is largely a price decline and a rising margin alone is a profitability trend.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProfitMoatDurability_x_CashEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(oiadp, at), 0.1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What makes cheapness safe is not this year's profitability but the demonstrated durability of excess returns on capital; a firm that has cleared a high operating-return hurdle in most of the last five years has a franchise the market is under-pricing when its cash-earnings yield is high, whereas a cheap firm that cleared it once is a cyclical fluke.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the EV-denominator family entirely and introduces a durability channel — a count of years above an absolute profitability hurdle — that is distinct from the level, trend, volatility, solvency and accrual moderators already in the archive: volatility rewards smoothness at any level and level rewards a single year, while this rewards sustained economic-moat evidence. The weight is a graded non-negative count from zero to five, so the signed cash-earnings yield leg, the valuation channel that produced every positive alpha so far, still governs the long and short sides.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ImprovingProfit_and_CheapCashYield_Conjunction
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: The mispriced group is firms that are simultaneously cheap on cash earnings and on an improving operating-return path; a firm must clear both bars, because a cheap firm with deteriorating returns is a trap and an improving firm at a rich price has the recovery already in the price.
considered.reasoning: Rather than repeating the short-side rank product whose low leg was an uninterpretable mixture, this puts the conjunction on the tail we actually trade: the top score requires both cheapness and fundamental improvement, and MIN cannot be replicated by any additive or multiplicative weighting because a strong leg cannot compensate for a weak one. It also isolates a specific design question against the archived DoubleScreen (which conjoined a static ROE with the same yield): does replacing the profitability *level* screen with a profitability *direction* screen raise the FF5 alpha, given that trend-weighted versions have consistently outperformed level-weighted ones in this archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MoatDurability_x_TotalCapitalEbitdaYield
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(oiadp, at), 0.1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A durable franchise is most mispriced when the whole capital structure, not just the equity, is priced cheaply against operating cash profit; the market discounts levered survivors with proven high returns on capital because it anchors on the debt rather than on the durability of the profit stream.
considered.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two strongest components — the durability count moderator (t-alpha 2.56) and the strictly positive total-capital yield that produced the best Sharpe (0.42) — to establish whether the durability effect is valuation-leg specific or additive across cheapness definitions. If both t-alpha and Sharpe exceed their parents, the two dimensions are complementary and this becomes the consolidation target for later generations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginDurability_x_CashEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(oiadp, sale), 0.1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Durable pricing power, measured as repeatedly sustaining a double-digit operating margin, is the moat dimension that protects a cheap stock, because margins persist through demand cycles whereas returns on assets can be inflated by a shrinking or written-down asset base.
considered.reasoning: This holds the valuation leg exactly equal to the archive's best signal and changes only the economic dimension of the durability hurdle from capital productivity to margin persistence, so the comparison directly identifies which kind of franchise evidence the market misprices. It also guards against a mechanical artifact in the winner: an asset-based hurdle can be cleared by asset write-downs, whereas a sales-based hurdle cannot.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MoatDurability_x_SignedYieldDeRating
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(oiadp, at), 0.1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), MA(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not a firm's permanent multiple but its displacement from its own normal multiple: a franchise with proven durable returns trading at a cash yield well above its own five-year average has been de-rated without fundamental cause, and the de-rating reverses.
considered.reasoning: The own-history family delivered the archive's largest alpha (2.5%) but a weak slope (fmb 1.86) precisely because a bounded TS_RANK leg makes the low-score side an ambiguous mixture; replacing it with a signed deviation from the firm's own five-year mean yield restores a genuinely two-sided spread where the short leg is unambiguously "re-rated above its own norm." Because the valuation state is firm-demeaned, it carries little HML loading, which is why this design produced high alpha in the first place.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AssetLightness_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Pricing a firm against its five-year average operating profit removes cyclical distortion from the cheapness measure, and such normalized cheapness is real value only for asset-light firms whose averaged profit is not an accounting illusion awaiting reinvestment.
considered.reasoning: A cycle-averaged earnings denominator is a valuation construction untested in this archive and is economically distinct from spot yields: it identifies firms cheap relative to mid-cycle earning power rather than firms cheap because this year happened to be good. Pairing it with capital lightness, the moderator with the archive's best Sharpe, tests whether normalization adds information beyond the spot yields used so far while keeping coverage high.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProfitInflection_x_CashEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(ACCEL(RATIO(oiadp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheap stocks re-rate at the inflection point, not at the trend reversal: when the rate of deterioration in operating returns stops worsening, the fundamental news that justified the low multiple has been exhausted, and the market is slow to recognize this second-derivative turn.
considered.reasoning: Acceleration is a temporal concept the archive has not tested — level, trend, volatility and durability all measure the state or its first derivative, whereas the inflection idea targets the moment the state stops deteriorating, which arrives earlier than a trend signal and should be less priced. The construction keeps the sign discipline that has worked throughout: a bounded non-negative rank weight on the proven cash-earnings-yield valuation leg, with only two lags required so coverage stays near the 0.13 level of the strongest signals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IntangibleCapitalIntensity_x_TotalCapitalEbitdaYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(xsga, 5), at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Selling and administrative spending is largely investment in brand, distribution and know-how that accounting expenses immediately, so firms with a large accumulated intangible outlay have systematically understated operating profit and capital; when such a firm already looks cheap on measured operating profit, its true economic yield is higher still and the market under-reacts to the hidden capital.
considered.reasoning: The instability is repaired at the source: the conditioner is now a cumulative five-year outlay scaled by total assets, a strictly non-negative quantity with a denominator that cannot approach zero or flip sign, so distressed firms with collapsed gross profit no longer contaminate the weight. The economic channel is also new to the archive — accounting mismeasurement of expensed intangible investment, rather than cost rigidity, durability, solvency, accruals or capital intensity — and it interacts specifically with a pre-depreciation profit yield that is depressed exactly for these firms, which is why neither leg alone captures the effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MoatDurability_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(oiadp, at), 0.1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness measured against mid-cycle earning power is most reliable for firms that have repeatedly cleared a high return-on-capital hurdle, because for them the five-year average profit is a franchise run-rate rather than a fading average of a deteriorating business.
considered.reasoning: This crosses the archive's best moderator (durability, t-alpha 2.49-2.56 across two valuation legs) with the valuation construction that just produced the archive's best result, and it is the single most likely combination to dominate both parents. It also answers a sharp question: the durability count was insensitive to spot-yield definitions, so if normalization lifts it materially, normalization and durability are attacking the same mispricing from complementary directions.

considered.name: AssetLightness_x_NormalEarningPowerOnCurrentCapital
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MUL(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5), at), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Normal earning power should be the firm's average return on capital applied to the capital it owns today, not its average historical dollar profit; measured this way, cheapness reflects the earning power of the current asset base and does not mechanically penalize firms that have grown.
considered.reasoning: This holds the moderator fixed at the winner's capital-lightness leg and changes only the normalization arithmetic, directly testing the critic's objection that averaged dollar earnings tilt against fast-growing firms in a way that masquerades as value. If the slope and alpha hold up or improve, the effect is genuinely about normalized earning power; if they collapse, the winner was partly a stale-growth tilt, which is essential to know before consolidating.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AssetLightness_x_NormalizedProfitToTotalCapital
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Because mid-cycle operating profit is the return to all capital providers, it should be priced against equity plus debt; doing so identifies levered firms whose normal earning power is cheap relative to the whole capital structure, a group equity-only yields misclassify as expensive.
considered.reasoning: The debt-inclusive denominator was the single change that produced the archive's best Sharpe in the spot-yield family (0.42), and normalization was the change that produced the best alpha, so this tests whether the two improvements are additive or whether they capture the same underlying correction. It is a controlled comparison against Signal 2 and the gen-3 winner, with the moderator and profit measure held constant so only the claim on capital differs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MoatDurability_x_EarningsShortfallFromNormal
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(oiadp, at), 0.1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(oiadp, 5), oiadp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Investors extrapolate the current year: a franchise firm whose profits are temporarily below their own five-year norm, with the shortfall large relative to market value, is priced as if the trough is permanent, and reversion to normal earning power is not in the price.
considered.reasoning: This is a new construct rather than another cheapness variant — the signal is the *gap* between normal and current earning power, scaled by market value, so it isolates cyclical depression rather than the level of the multiple, and it is only economically sensible when gated by evidence that the firm's high returns are durable, which the count supplies. It also directly tests the reversion assumption embedded in the normalized-yield winner: if the alpha comes from reversion of depressed earnings, this signal should carry it in concentrated form.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AboveIndustryMarginPersistence_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(oiadp, sale)), 0), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The durability that protects a cheap stock is competitive rather than absolute: what matters is how many of the last five years the firm out-earned its own industry on margin, since that measures a defended position rather than membership of a structurally high-margin sector.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the flagged weakness in the absolute 10% margin hurdle, which can proxy for industry membership, by counting years of above-industry margin instead, and it keeps the valuation leg identical to Signal 1 so the comparison isolates the hurdle definition. A cleaner franchise measure should raise the cross-sectional slope, which was the weaker metric for the margin-durability version (fmb 2.84).

considered.name: MoatDurability_x_PeakEarningPowerYield
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(oiadp, at), 0.1), 5), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_MAX(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: For a firm with demonstrated franchise durability, the best anchor for value is the profit it has proven it can earn at the top of its own cycle; when today's price is low relative to that proven peak, the market is capitalizing the trough of a business that has already shown a higher ceiling.
considered.reasoning: Peak earning power is a different valuation anchor from the average — it is robust to a string of weak years dragging the mean down and it emphasizes demonstrated capability rather than central tendency — so this maps the normalization dimension rather than re-scaling it. The durability gate is essential here, because for firms without proven high returns a five-year maximum is a one-off windfall and the signal would degenerate into a stale-peak trap.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AssetLightness_x_SpotOperatingEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(oiadp, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: If both the cycle-average level of earning power and the current excess over that average are priced too cheaply, then the simple spot operating-earnings yield — which is exactly their sum — should carry the combined effect, and it should do so most strongly for asset-light firms whose reported operating profit is not consumed by reinvestment.
considered.reasoning: This is the decisive decomposition test for the whole normalized-yield family: the archive shows the averaged component predicts positively (t 3.55) and the deviation component predicts positively once its sign is corrected (implied t 3.34), so their sum should dominate unless the two components' portfolio exposures offset. It costs no coverage — no five-year lag is required — which also tells us whether the champion's five-lag requirement was buying anything.

considered.name: OwnNormProfitSurprise_x_NormalizedEarningsYield

considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 3), csho), 3), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: CapitalProductivity_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: AssetLightness_x_ConservativeEarningPowerYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MIN(oiadp, MA(oiadp, 5)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: FiveYearCashValidation_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 5), at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: AssetLightness_x_TroughEarningPowerYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_MIN(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: AssetLightness_x_NormalizedResidualEarningPowerYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(SUB(oiadp, xint), 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: LighteningCapitalBase_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3), 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: VariableCostFlexibility_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(cogs, ADD(cogs, xsga))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: CapitalEfficientGrowth_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(sale, 5), GROWTH(at, 5)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: LiquidityBuffer_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: LiquidAndAssetLight_Conjunction_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, at)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

It is the appropriate structure if the mechanism is a survival-and-retention requirement rather than a graded characteristic.

considered.name: LiquidityBuffer_x_OperatingBusinessPriceYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MAX(SUB(MUL(prcc_f, csho), che), ceq)), 1)))

considered.name: FinancialSlackShare_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))

considered.name: CapitalReplacementRunway_x_NormalizedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, dp), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The balance-sheet condition that protects normalized cheapness is how many years of capital replacement a firm could fund from cash already in hand; a cheap firm with several years of runway will reach the recovery in its mid-cycle earning power without raising outside money, while one whose cash covers only months of capital consumption must dilute or borrow first.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the dimensionally incoherent stock-minus-flow difference with a ratio of two dollar quantities whose quotient has a genuine unit — years of replacement capital funded — and it is not a relabeling of cash intensity, because it equals cash-to-assets divided by depreciation-to-assets and therefore moves with both winning conditioners rather than either alone. considered.name: LiquidAssets_Plus_NormalizedEarningsYield_Composite
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(che, at), RATIO(MA(oiadp, 5), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))
considered.hypothesis: If liquid balance-sheet composition genuinely strengthens cheapness rather than merely adding to it, then the multiplicative conditioning form should beat an equally weighted composite of the same two ingredients; the composite is the honest benchmark, and it is a defensible signal in its own right because it buys firms that are cheap on mid-cycle earning power, liquid, or both.

Its portfolio will also be far less concentrated than the product's, so if it matches the product's alpha with a higher Sharpe the additive form is the better final recommendation, and if it falls materially short the interaction claim is confirmed.
